title: why it's said three times
hookLine: a teacher and student ask for peace before the lesson: why shanti is said three times
last: COUNT WHAT YOU WANT TO KEEP.

lines: TEACHER AND STUDENT, BEFORE THE LESSON.
cards: In the old forest schools, a lesson didn't begin with the lesson. Teacher and student first said a prayer together, one still chanted today. May we both be protected.
May we both be nourished. May we work together with strength. May our study shine.
May we never turn against each other. Then they closed it the way many Hindu prayers close: om shanti shanti shanti. Not once.
Three times. Traditional teachers read the three as a list.

teach.b: Shanti means peace, the settled kind: calm water with nothing stirring it. The Bhagavad Gita puts it bluntly: for someone without peace, how can there be happiness? Now the three.
Traditional teachers read the three shantis as three kinds of trouble, the three places a bad day can come from.
Trouble from forces beyond anyone's control: storms, floods, the world.
Trouble from other beings: the friend who didn't call, the driver who cut in.
And trouble from within: your own body and your own mind. Three sources, three shantis. The teachers add something practical.
There's little anyone can do about the first, more about the second, and the third is the one most within reach, and the easiest to skip. So the chant isn't padding.

It goes down the list: peace out there, peace between us, peace in here. So when a family ends its prayer this way, or a teacher and student end their chant, they're asking for peace in all three places at once.

how: Hindu prayers, readings and ceremonies often close with om shanti shanti shanti, the word for peace said three times.

games.q: Nani's last night 😢 we did aarti and she ended with om shanti shanti shanti. Sam whispered 'why 3 times, is it like an echo?'
o: not an echo. three shantis: peace from the world, peace with other people, peace in your own mind. the last one's most in reach.
it's three wishes, like birthday candles.
games.why: Teacher and student closed their peace chant with shanti three times. Traditional teachers read the three as peace from the world, from other beings, and within.

s: shanti is said three times just for the rhythm
traditional teachers read the three as three sources of trouble: the world, others, and yourself.
the Gita asks how someone without peace can be happy
Bhagavad Gita 2.66: without peace, how can there be happiness?

games.q: someone cuts you off in traffic. then you replay it in your head for the next hour. which shanti does the hour of replay need?
games.why: the driver was other people. the hour of replay is the third, your own mind, the one that's most within reach.

games.q: put the three shantis in order, the way the teachers read them.

practice: Three breaths with the bell, one shanti on each, said silently. First out-breath: toward the world. Second: toward one person you're not at peace with.
You don't have to forgive them. Third: toward your own mind.

wordCard.voice: Shanti. Peace, the settled kind, said three times: the world, other people, your own mind. Fourteenth word. Puja, dharma, atman, Brahman, guru, japa, shanti: that's week two.

orig.note: Sanskrit: peace, calm, quiet. said three times at the close of the peace chants.

carryVoice: Your line: peace, peace, peace. Next time something rattles you, there are three places it could have come from. Next week brings the doing words. Day fourteen.

sources.ref: Peace chant saha navavatu (Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1; also the Katha Upanishad's invocation), closing om shanti shanti shanti
